records.title: Scanning into a recursive struct
records.body:
Hi,

I'd like to scan into a recursive struct:
```go
type Node struct {
	ID       string
	Parent   *Node
}
var nodes []*Node
err := sqlscan.Select(ctx, conns.PgClient, &nodes, `select id, null as parent from nodes where parent_id is null`)
```
This causes an infinite loop as scany introspects struct recursively.

Any tips for achieving that? I might be missing something obvious since I'm new to Go and scany. Ideally I'd like not to touch the Node struct definition since in my real-life code it is auto-generated. Also I'd like to avoid using `db:"-"` on Parent since I might want to get the immediate parent with a join.

Thanks!

records.title: Implement mutual recursion TCO on JavaScript
`GenerateModuleMetadata` / `GenerateMavenPom` triggers slow graph traversal during configuration cache serialisation with `fromResolutionResult()`
records.body: ### Current Behavior When `versionMapping { fromResolutionResult() }` is enabled ([which we use in a number of our plugins](https://github.com/palantir/gradle-consistent-versions/blame/3.8.0/src/main/java/com/palantir/gradle/versions/VersionsPropsPlugin.java#L345-L355)), configuration cache serialisation of `GenerateModuleMetadata` and `GenerateMavenPom` tasks becomes extremely slow. The slowdown scales quadratically (I think) with the combination of dependency graph size and number of dependencies/constraints. For example, in a 150-module project with ~4000 dependency constraints per module: - Without `fromResolutionResult()`: CC store time ~1s - With `fromResolutionResult()`: CC store time ~30-40s In larger real-world projects, we've observed a worst case store times of 2h 6m 23s storing a 40.4 MiB cache entry — that's roughly 5 KiB/s. ### Expected Behavior Configuration cache serialisation should complete in a reasonable time regardless of whether `fromResolutionResult()` is enabled. The version mapping resolution should be cached or performed more efficiently. ### Context (optional) This issue was discovered while rolling out configuration cache to ~1,500 repositories. We had to roll back due to this slowdown. Here are some screenshots from the worst offenders (apologies that I can't link to the build scans directly — this is all internal/non-public code): This build spent 2h 6m 23s storing a 40.4 MiB cache entry — that's roughly 5 KiB/s. The model configuration itself only took 19.5s, yet storing the configuration cache took over 2 hours (ran on a mac book pro M2):. Here's another CI build that spent 5m 30s storing a 133.2 MiB cache — approximately 0.4 MB/s. Configuration caching accounts for over 70% of the total configuration time (6m 8s out of 8m 41s). Without configuration cache enabled the configuration phase only take a couple of minutes on this repo. Before I had to rolled this back, I gathered some data across the fleet. Below are graphs using data extracted from build scans on CI runs: Key observations from rollout: * The storage rate distribution shows most repos writing at under 1 MB/s, with a heavy concentration below 0.5 MB/s * Most repos peak around 15–20% of configuration time spent on configuration caching, but there's a long tail extending past 60% Key observations from profiling: - The bottleneck is in `DefaultResolvedComponentResult.eachElement()` - JFR profiling shows `eachElement()` consuming ~29,000 samples over ~5.5 minutes during CC storage - The expensive computation is triggered during serialisation via `Cached$Deferred.writeReplace()` Stack trace pattern: ``` Cached$Deferred.writeReplace → GenerateModuleMetadata.computeInputState / GenerateMavenPom → ModuleMetadataSpecBuilder.dependencyConstraintsFor / MavenComponentParser.getDependenciesForVariant → VersionMappingComponentDependencyResolver.maybeResolveVersion → DefaultResolvedComponentResult.eachElement (recursive - full graph traversal?) ``` **Root cause hypothesis**: `VersionMappingComponentDependencyResolver.maybeResolveVersion()` performs a full dependency graph traversal via `eachElement()` for every single dependency/constraint, with no caching between calls. This results in O(n × m) complexity where n = graph size and m = number of dependencies/constraints. Impact: - Users see builds take longer with CC enabled than without - CI builds always hit cache misses (no persistent cache), paying the store cost every run - Disabling tasks doesn't help - disabled tasks are still serialised by CC This is particularly painful for our use case: we need to run with configuration cache enabled on CI to validate that users haven't broken configuration cache compatibility, but since CI environments don't persist the cache between runs, we'll always hit a miss. This means we pay the cost of storing the cache on every build but never see any benefit from it. We also publish to maven local as part of build which adds the (disabled) `generateMetadataFileFor*Publication` tasks to the graph ### Self-contained Reproducer Project https://github.com/FinlayRJW/gmm-cc-reproducer To reproduce: `git clone https://github.com/FinlayRJW/gmm-cc-reproducer` `cd gmm-cc-reproducer` Clear CC and run - observe slow store time in build scan `rm -rf .gradle/configuration-cache && ./gradlew generatePomFileForMavenPublication --configuration-cache --dry-run --scan` To compare: Comment out `fromResolutionResult()` in `build.gradle` and re-run. ### Gradle version 9.2.1 on reproducer, 8.14.3 internally ### Build scan URL (optional) I can't get a build scan due to network restrictions but you should be able to generate one with the reproducer ### Your Environment (optional) Model Name: MacBook Pro Chip: Apple M2 Pro Total Number of Cores: 10 (6 performance and 4 efficiency) Memory: 32 GB Gradle 8.14.3 / 9.2.1

records.title: Type-check dependent files too
records.body:
# Problem
Currently, `tsc-files` will receive a list of files as arguments and will only type-check them.

Suppose you have the following two files:
```ts
// types.ts
export type User = {
  name: string
}
```
```ts
// index.ts
import { User } from './foo'

const user: User = {
  name: 'John Doe'
}
```

Everything OK. But now imagine you apply some change to `types.ts` that would break `index.ts`:
```diff
-   name: string
+   fullName: string
```

And then you run `tsc-files` with `lint-staged`, so that `tsc-files` will only receive the files that were changed (`index.ts` won't be type-checked because it wasn't changed). In that case, `tsc-files` won't alert you that `index.ts` is broken.

# Possible solution
To fix that behavior, `tsc-files` should be able to type-check not only the files given as arguments but also **all files that recursively depend on those**.

records.title: Allow dynamically-recursive child module references with count and for_each
records.body:
Hi there tf team,

tl;dr, recursive modules generate an error on `terraform init`.
~Not sure if bug or feature request.~ Feature request.

```
module "xyz" {
  source = "./"
}
```

### Terraform Version

```
Terraform v0.14.2
```

### Terraform Configuration Files

Please see [demo](https://github.com/willscripted/terraform-recursion-error). Since it is an issue with modules, there are multiple files to show. The module definition at [`dir/main.tf#L4-10`](https://github.com/willscripted/terraform-recursion-error/blob/main/dir/main.tf#L4-L10) is the section generating the error.

```terraform
module "dir" {
  source = "./"
  for_each = { for file in local.root_filesystem : file.name => file if file.type == "dir" }

  name = each.key
  children = each.value.children
}
```

### [Debug Output](https://github.com/willscripted/terraform-recursion-error/blob/main/debug.txt)

### Crash Output

No `crash.log` found.

### Expected Behavior

Successful `terraform init`.

### Actual Behavior

Init failed, appears to be when stack depth exceeds some thresholds. (Props to whoever added that failsafe; it's much easier to track down when the process terminates.)

### Steps to Reproduce

```
git clone git@github.com:willscripted/terraform-recursion-error.git
cd terraform-recursion-error
terraform init
```

### Additional Context

Nothing special. Out-of-the-box hashicorp/terraform container.

### References

VladRassokhin touches on it right at the end of #15276. His #22648 issue is closely related to this. The rest of an [`is:issue recursion`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues?q=is%3Aissue+recursion) search does not look relevant.

records.title: Mutually Recursive Modules
records.body:
In section 5, the report says that mutually recursive modules must be supported:

> Modules may be mutually recursive

but then doesn't say how to use it:

> separate compilation of mutually recursive modules may require that imported modules contain additional information so that they may be referenced before they are compiled

Saying that a feature must be supported but not explaining how to use it is bizarre and probably should be changed. Here's three different options on how this could be changed:

* A) Change the wording to say that implementations, may but are not required to support mutually recursive modules
* B) Codify GHC's `.hs-boot` files into the report
* C) Say that implementations must fully support mutually recursive modules and say that GHC's implementation is buggy

In [Hazy](https://github.com/superstar64/hazy), I currently fully support mutual recursive modules without any additional hassle and completely ignore `.hs-boot` files, so I would prefer to avoid B.

records.title: `ipfs pin add` on large trees is extremely slow even when most of the content is already pinned
records.body:
#### Version information:
    go-ipfs version: 0.4.13-
    Repo version: 6
    System version: amd64/linux
    Golang version: go1.9.4

#### Type:
Enhancement

#### Description:
`ipfs pin add` is slow on large data sets, because it needs to walk the entire tree in order to verify that it exists on the node (and, if not, fetch it from elsewhere) before the pin is considered successful. This is expected.

However, it looks like when pinning something *that itself contains other pinned objects*, it re-checks all of the contents, even though it should know that the contents are already present.

Reproduction:

    hash=$(ipfs add <a whole lot of data>)
    ipfs pin ls --type=recursive  # should output hash
    ipfs files mkdir /test
    ipfs files cp /ipfs/$hash /test/foo
    ipfs pin add $(ipfs files stat --hash /test)

The call to `ipfs pin add` will take as long as the original `ipfs add` did, or nearly so, even though all that data is already pinned and known to be present.

Ideally, `pin add` -- or whatever underlying function it calls to make sure the data is all available in the node -- should be smart enough to realize that when it encounters a recursively pinned object, it doesn't need to traverse that object's children, as they are guaranteed to be present.

records.title: [JENKINS-33239] Environment variable resolves variables recursively
records.body:
The function hudson.Util.replaceMacro(String, ...) resolves recursively properties, such as:
PATH=path1:$PATH
into
PATH=path1:path1:path1:path1:path1:path1:path1:path1:path1:path1:path1:path1:path1:path1:path1: etc.

I encountered it when setting variables for slave and running multijob with envinject - the variables were calculated and passed to the child jobs and resulted in running out of memory. More precisely with this variable:
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$ORACLE_HOME/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

I would expect Jenkins to resolve the R-value and push it in L-value, not to resolve it over and over again.

Note: I didn't set the variable like this, I suppose it was meant to take $LD_LIBRARY_PATH from Linux server settings and append $ORACLE_HOME/lib

Note2: Version 1.580.3 ran with those variables fine.

records.title: Graph visualization mode (nodes and edges, not just grids)
records.body:
## Branch
`feat/graph-visualization`

## Why
Grids are a special case of graphs. A general graph visualizer with draggable nodes and weighted/directed edges unlocks an entire class of algorithms that don't map to grids: Bellman-Ford, Kruskal's MST, Prim's MST, graph coloring, cycle detection, and strongly connected components. It's the natural evolution beyond the grid-based pathfinding mode.

## Files
- `src/types/index.ts` — add `GraphNode`, `GraphEdge`, `GraphData`, `GraphStep` interfaces, add `'graph'` to category and step unions
- `src/components/visualizers/GraphVisualizer.tsx` — new component: canvas-based graph renderer with force-directed or manual node positioning
- `src/hooks/useGraphRenderer.ts` — new hook: manages canvas rendering of graph structures (node circles, edge lines/arrows, labels, highlighting)
- `src/hooks/useGraphManagement.ts` — new hook: manages graph state (add/remove nodes, add/remove edges, set weights, drag nodes)
- `src/algorithms/graphBfs.ts` — new file: BFS on adjacency list with step generation
- `src/algorithms/graphDfs.ts` — new file: DFS on adjacency list with step generation
- `src/algorithms/index.ts` — import and register graph algorithms
- `src/components/VisualizationArea.tsx` — add routing for `'graph'` step type to `GraphVisualizer`
- `src/components/controls/GraphControls.tsx` — new component: add node, add edge, set directed/undirected, set weighted, graph presets
- `src/App.tsx` — render `GraphControls` in sidebar when in graph mode
- `src/utils/colorUtils.ts` — add graph node/edge color states
- `src/utils/graphUtils.ts` — new file: adjacency list helpers, graph presets (complete graph, cycle, bipartite, random)

## Tasks
1. [ ] In `src/types/index.ts`: add `GraphNode` interface: `{ id: string, label: string, x: number, y: number }`. Add `GraphEdge` interface: `{ from: string, to: string, weight?: number, directed?: boolean }`. Add `GraphData` interface: `{ nodes: GraphNode[], edges: GraphEdge[], directed: boolean, weighted: boolean }`. Add `GraphStep` interface: `{ type: 'graph', graph: GraphData, visitedNodes?: string[], visitedEdges?: string[], currentNode?: string, currentEdge?: string, frontierNodes?: string[], message?: string, stats?: AlgorithmStats }`. Add `'graph'` to `AlgorithmCategory` and `GraphStep` to `AlgorithmStep`
2. [ ] Create `src/utils/graphUtils.ts`: export graph construction helpers — `createGraph(directed, weighted): GraphData`, `addNode(graph, label, x, y)`, `addEdge(graph, from, to, weight?)`, `removeNode(graph, id)`, `removeEdge(graph, from, to)`, `getNeighbors(graph, nodeId)`, `getAdjacencyList(graph)`. Export preset generators: `createCompleteGraph(n)`, `createCycleGraph(n)`, `createBipartiteGraph(m, n)`, `createRandomGraph(n, edgeProbability)` — each positions nodes in a circle or grid layout
3. [ ] Create `src/hooks/useGraphManagement.ts`: manage `GraphData` state. Provide `addNode`, `addEdge`, `removeNode`, `removeEdge`, `setDirected`, `setWeighted`, `moveNode(id, x, y)` for drag interactions, `loadPreset(type)`, and `clearGraph`. Generate unique IDs for nodes
4. [ ] Create `src/hooks/useGraphRenderer.ts`: accept `canvasRef`, `step: GraphStep`, `containerSize`, `onNodeDrag` callback. Render loop: draw edges as lines (undirected) or arrows (directed) with optional weight labels at midpoint, draw nodes as circles with labels centered. Apply highlight colors for `visitedNodes`, `visitedEdges`, `currentNode`, `frontierNodes`. Handle mouse events: click to select node, drag to move node (update position via callback), double-click canvas to add node. Support dark/light mode
5. [ ] Create `src/components/visualizers/GraphVisualizer.tsx`: canvas element in responsive container. Accept `step` and graph management callbacks. Forward to `useGraphRenderer`
6. [ ] Create `src/algorithms/graphBfs.ts`: BFS traversal on adjacency list following the `Algorithm` pattern. The `generate` function accepts `GraphData`, traverses using a queue from a start node. Emit `GraphStep` objects with cumulative `visitedNodes` and `visitedEdges`, `currentNode` for the node being processed, `frontierNodes` for the queue. Track `nodesVisited` in stats. Messages: "Visiting node A", "Adding neighbor B to queue"
7. [ ] Create `src/algorithms/graphDfs.ts`: DFS traversal following the same pattern. Use a stack (or recursion with explicit stack for steps). Messages reference the stack state
8. [ ] Register graph algorithms in `src/algorithms/index.ts` with `category: 'graph'`
9. [ ] Update `src/components/VisualizationArea.tsx`: add conditional render for `'graph'` step type routing to `<GraphVisualizer>`

records.title: Spec: Narrow reviewer intent to the exact action (define scope as blast radius)
records.body:
## Problem Statement

In a long implementation session, delegated review judges **the surrounding task’s intent**, not the **exact action’s intent**, then hard-denies ordinary asks.

A recorded Pi session (`01a00d7a-ae27-7e63-8a50-43beac856df0`) asked to read a local Herdr skill file and to run Herdr inspect commands. Those asks correctly reach safe-allow. The reviewer then treated “implement Issue #50” as the thing being authorized and scored:

- `riskLevel = high` because the session is an implementation program
- `scope = broad` because that program is a large feature, not because the exact payload is wide

The Guardian code floor then denies whenever `riskLevel` is `high` and `scope` is not `narrow`, even when `userAuthorization` is already `high`. Several recorded denials were allow-shaped rationales that the floor rewrote after it saw `high` + task-width `broad`.

This is a judgment-window defect on an already-routed `ask`. Grilling transcripts filling the assistant evidence budget were one recorded *symptom* of a wide window, not the problem to specify.

### What `scope` is

`scope` is a required reviewer field: `narrow` or `broad`. The shipped instructions only list it in the JSON shape. The shipped policy never defines the two values. The code floor treats `scope !== "narrow"` as a hard deny for `high` risk.

**Intended meaning (this spec makes it explicit):** `scope` is the **blast radius of the exact action in the dossier** — how many targets, how unbounded the destination, how many unrelated side effects are in *this* payload.

| `scope` | Means | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| `narrow` | One inspectable target or one fully present command whose effects stay inside that target | `read` of a single installed skill file; `herdr pane current --current`; one local test script |
| `broad` | The exact payload itself is unbounded, many-target, or bundles unrelated side effects | wildcard / recursive delete; opaque `eval` whose leaves are unknown; `verify && git commit` when commit was not the asked step; export whose destination is unresolved |

**Not `scope`:** whether the issue, grilling tree, or session goal is a large feature. That is task narrative. It may inform `userAuthorization` (“the user asked to implement #50”). It must not set `scope=broad` and must not raise `riskLevel`.

### Diagnosis: model error vs rule gap

The recorded `high` + `broad` is **wrong for the product intent** and **coherent with the prompt the reviewer was given**. The primary fix is the contract and the intent window, not swapping the reviewer model, not removing the high-risk authorization floor, and not adding a second code oracle that re-derives `scope` from dossier facts.

**What the rules already said, and the model missed.** Default instructions open with “one exact Pi action.” Default policy opens with “Judge the exact action.” The four high-risk themes are exfil, credential probing, persistent weakening, and destruction. A local skill-file read and `herdr pane current` are not in those classes. The same session already produced the right class of verdict: the earlier skill-file read was `low`; after the user said allow, the same `SKILL.md` became `medium`. At 05:44 it scored the task instead.

**What the rules made easy.** Three gaps, of which this spec closes the first two. The third is the existing floor behaving as written — it is not a second feature to rewrite.

1. **`scope` is undefined.** The field is required. The model invents “the issue is large.”
2. **The intent window contradicts the first sentence.** The same prompt says judge the exact action and then ships the whole session as authorization evidence. Raising `riskLevel` and setting `scope=broad` follows the second instruction.
3. **The floor then denies.** `high` + non-`narrow` is rewritten to deny even when authorization is already `high` and the rationale is allow-shaped. That is correct given today’s contract. After (1) and (2), the model should emit `narrow` (and usually not `high`) for a single-file read, so this clause stops firing on task width.

| Recorded fact | Owner |
|---|---|
| “Implement #50” becomes the judged object | Rules: window too wide |
| `scope=broad` on a single-file read | Rules: field undefined |
| `riskLevel=high` on a skill read / `pane current` | Primarily the window; secondarily the model dropping the first sentence |
| High authorization still denied | Existing floor, given the polluted `scope` |
| 02:10 correct, 05:44 wrong, allow-then-correct | Model is context-sensitive; rules never pin intent to this ask |

Re-deriving narrowness from dossier facts in the floor would also have unblocked 05:44, but it is a **fallback second source of truth** for `scope`. This spec does not add that oracle. One mechanism: pin what the reviewer is allowed to judge, and define the field it must fill.

## Solution

One change: **narrow the intent the reviewer may judge**, and **define `scope` so that field has only one meaning**.

1. **Define `scope`** in default instructions and policy as exact-action blast radius (table above). Task width is not `scope`. Session narrative may change `userAuthorization` only. It must not raise `riskLevel` or set `scope=broad`.
2. **Pin the intent window.** The reviewer may use exact action facts plus the current user authorization that covers this ask. Earlier session goals, design-tree Q&A, and implement-skill prose are not the judged object. How evidence is packed is an implementation choice in service of this window, not a product rule about grilling or assistant character caps.

Keep the existing Guardian floor as-is:

```text
if absoluteDeny or riskLevel == critical → deny
if riskLevel == high and (scope != narrow or auth not in {medium, high}) → deny
else honor reviewer verdict
```

Do not add a parallel “factually narrow according to dossier facts” override. After the window and definition land, a single-file read should come back `narrow` (and typically low or medium). The floo
